newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: MINISTER CALLS FOR MORE MINING LAND
The Federal Resources Minister, Warwick Parer, wants to see more wilderness land available for mining.
Senator Parer released a report, showing Australia expects to earn A$37 billion from its mineral resource exports in 1996-97.
He says some areas open themselves up to multiple land use that's environmentally sensible and culturally and socially acceptable.
The Government is reviewing the Native Title legislation and environmental laws, but Senator Parer says there's still much uncertainty about where mining will be allowed.
Federal Environment Mininster, Robert Hill, says the Government supports multiple land use, but the more you interfere with wilderness areas the less they become wilderness.
CHINA RENEWS ATTACKS OVER DALAI LAMA
China has launched another attack on Australia over the Dalai Lama.
A commentary in the state-run media described the decisions of John Howard and Alexander Downer to meet him as "absurd," and said such talks meant interference in China's internal affairs.
The commentary, carried by the official Xinhua news agency, said Mr Howard and Mr Downer had deserted Australia's policy of recognising Tibet as a part of China.

Beijing has repeatedly warned of the damage that would be done to Sino-Australian ties, particularly economic and trade links. The prime minister is scheduled to have talks with the Dalai Lama tomorrow.
BEAZLEY ON PRIME MINISTER'S CHINA TROUBLES
The Federal Opposition Leader says the drama over the Prime Minister's planned meeting with the Dalai Lama and its effect on Australia's relationship with China has been blown out of proportion.
Beijing has threatened to take action against Australian companies doing business in China if Mr Howard goes meets with the exiled tibetan spiritual leader tomorrow.
Opposition Leader Kim Beazley says Australia's relationship with China deteoriated when the Howard Government dishonoured an agreement with China under the so-called DIFF overseas aid scheme.
Mr Beazley says Mr Howard should meet with the Dalai Lama and find other ways of bettering the relationship with China.
He says the restoration of the DIFF scheme and other such programmes would be a start to repairing ties with China.
COUNCIL LOSES FIGHT OVER SYDNEY AIRPORT DEVELOPMENT
A Sydney council has lost Federal Court action against a billion dollar development plan for Sydney Airport.

Marrickville Council argued that the Federal Government should have commissioned an environmental impact statement for the 15 year plan, which includes tripling the number of aircraft gates and extending the major passenger terminals.
Justice Susan Keifel, who reviewed the decision not to commission an Environmental Impact Study, says there's no basis for setting it aside.
BLACKHAWK AIR INQUIRY CONTINUES

An inquiry in Perth has heard how inaccuracies in a hand-drawn map presented during a briefing to personnel before the Blackhawk air disaster made no difference to the outcome of the ill-fated exercise.
The Military Inquiry is hearing evidence about the accident near Townsville in June which claimed 18 lives.

A sergeant with the Special Air Services has told the inquiry a diagram of the area where the exercise was held was different to photographs of the site. He was on board one of six Blackhawks involved in the exercise.

He said the inaccuracies in the map did not affect his ability to conduct the counter-terrorist training exercise, claiming SAS soldiers were trained to deal with mistakes in this type of information.
FEARS FOR STOLEN GENERATION INQUIRY
The President of the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission has expressed deep anxiety over the future of the Stolen Generation inquiry and the fate of its report, due by the end of the year.
Sir Ronald Wilson says the Government is due to present evidence to the inquiry but has failed to respond to repeated invitations.
He says without the help of the Federal Government the inquiry will lack vital information concerning the past practice of separating indigenous children from their families.
Sir Ronald acknowledged support the inquiry had received from state and territory governments and also the Federal Department of Health and Family Services.
COLES NOT TO DISTRIBUTE PAPERS ON SOLOMON LEW
Coles Myer has agreed not to read or disseminate papers involving its director Solomon Lew, until legal action in the Federal Court is settled.
The documents it currently possesses relate to evidence about the so-called Yannon transactions.
Mr Lew, his lieutenant Harry Cooper and lawyer, Monica Ellen Vinson earlier this year gave evidence at the Australian Securities Commission which was investigating the 18-million dollar transaction.
Those documents were released by the Commission to Coles Myer and legal action is now underway.
The next preliminary hearing has been set down for October.
-- Sydney Reuters newsroom 61-2 373 1800
